So I think the first thing we should do is we should just set for people who are not familiar with it, a broad overview of the Competes Act. We could call it Competes. We can call it USICCA. It's had a lot of names at various points in its life, endless frontier, I think. But what are the main points of the Act? But what are some of the main things this act is trying to accomplish?

Right. So for the listeners, There's two separate bills, actually. The United States Innovation and Competition Act that the Senate passed several months ago, and then there's an America Compete Act that the House passed. And the Conference Committee is about merging these two bills into a single bill that can pass both the House and Senate and get sent to the President's desk. The basic elements that are in both bills are, we face the semiconductor shortage. So there's a bill called the CHIPS Act that is broadly supported, Democrats, Republicans, House and Senate that would help ensure the semiconductor industry and rebuild it here in the United States. We invented semiconductors. We used to be the world's leader in semiconductors. But over the years, a lot of that production has been outsourced. We're seeing the impact of not having an adequate supply of semiconductors because they're in everything. They're in cars, they're in your microwave, they're in your cell phones, pretty much everything that we use every day. And part of the reason why you're seeing inflation is the lack of this basic ingredient of all of our daily purchases, semiconductors. So we want to bring that back, and we've talked to companies all around the world that will locate their manufacturing of semiconductors here in the United States if we can pass that CHPSAC. So that'll be in the final bill. Other key areas in both bills are addressing supply chain issues. We talked about semiconductors, but we've seen with the pandemic lots of disruption in supply chains, raw ingredients, et cetera. So this will help us address some of that. Some of the more contentious issues are, you know, we have some climate provisions in there that will those stay in the final bill will see. You know, there's different dollar amounts to invest in the National Science Foundation and research. I think that'll be in there what the final dollar amounts and how those dollars get allocated, you know, that's still being negotiated. At the end of the day, I'm pretty optimistic that we'll get a final bill done hopefully in July before the August recess and get that sent to the President's desk.

turn_text: you sit at a really interesting spot here because you are on the space subcommittee and the science and technology committees, and you're also on the committee for foreign affairs. And so you are kind of at this intersection of tech policy and science and then also foreign policy. I'm curious because something we think a lot about on this show is the broader struggle between the world of liberal democracy and the world of illiberalism and authoritarianism, like you see in Russia and China, and they're becoming more aggressive. I'm curious how you see that playing out and how the US tech policy in general influences this battle between liberalism and illiberalism.

I guess let me frame it this way. When I think about the 75 years post-World War II, it was a relatively peaceful and prosperous time for the globe. And we can be very proud of what we did as the United States in helping rebuild Europe, helping rebuild Japan, working with Korea, You have to take it from one of the poorest countries in the world to the 10 largest economy in the world. You had relative peace and stability. You didn't have big country kinetic conflicts the way you did prior to World War II on a fairly regular basis. I think we got used to that model where the United States really was dictating the path forward and we were the only superpower and the world relied on us. We're not coming out of two real back-to-back disruptive events, the first being the pandemic, which really brought the world to the standstill for two and a half years. And now big country invasions, being Russia invading Ukraine. And those two events so close together have really disrupted a global world order. I think when I think about the next 75 years, I think we have to think about it in the context that maybe the last 75 years was anomaly. And historically, you do see these disruptive events. And I think in that context, when we think about economy, when we think about foreign policy, you're starting to see realignments where you talk to the Japanese today. They're much more outward looking and much more interested in their own geopolitical strategy and defense. The Koreans are starting to look outward. with the invasion of Ukraine by Russia, the Europeans are going to have to be much more interested in their own security. And I think you're seeing a multilateral coalition of liberal democracies free market economies coming together. On the other side, You see an autocrat like Vladimir Putin, an autocrat like Xi Jinping, which is a very different economic top-down model of economic policy but also of governance. And I think you will see this clash of these two different models. I think we're going to win because I do think, you know, the top down model has never been one of success over the long haul because it doesn't necessarily invite innovation, free thinking entrepreneurship. and people at the end of the day want freedoms to determine their own path forward. But it's not a given. And I think that's where we have to work with our like-minded, like-valued allies to win the next 75 years.
